# MemBridge: full site content for LLMs

> This file contains the complete content of https://membridge.app/ in plain markdown, for AI assistants and crawlers. Short version: https://membridge.app/llms.txt

## What is MemBridge?

MemBridge is shared team memory for AI coding agents. It watches every Claude Code and Codex session on a team, distills what each one worked out, and gets it to everyone else's agents: at startup, mid-session, and on demand.

Headline: **Your teammates' agents already know what yours figured out.**

It is a background daemon on each developer's machine plus a desktop app for the team view. Free to install with no account, source-available, four small runtime dependencies (libsodium-wrappers, web-tree-sitter, the MCP SDK, zod), no build step, Node 18+. Claude Code and Codex adapters are built in.

## The problem it solves

Every AI coding session starts from zero, and every developer's agents are blind to what their teammates' agents already worked out. We measured how much this costs: across 6,104 real agent sessions from 310 developers, the median developer spends 31% of their tokens re-orienting an agent in code it has already seen. See The Context Ledger: https://membridge.app/context-ledger/

## How it reaches your agents: three moments

1. **At startup.** What the team's agents worked out gets written into the instruction files your agents already read (`CLAUDE.md`, `AGENTS.md`), attributed by person. Every session opens briefed. Nobody writes a doc.
2. **Mid-session.** Your agent opens a file a teammate's agent made a call about, and that call enters the running session. Once, exactly when it matters. No doc, no Slack, no human relaying it.
3. **On demand.** A ranked search over what every agent on the team has actually done, exposed over MCP so any agent can query it directly. It ranks across the decisions people made, the gotchas they hit, what they were trying to do and the files they touched, filterable by teammate, project, file or date. Ranked by relevance, not recency: the useful answer is usually months old.

## The desktop app

The app shows the team from the outside: every agent session across the team, who can see which project, and where knowledge is concentrated in one person's head.

- **Today**: who is live right now with the ask each session opened with, plus per-project activity for the week.
- **Projects**: a who-sees-what grid. Tick a cell to grant or revoke access without opening the project. Private projects cannot be granted until they are shared. Every change lands in the audit trail.
- **Members**: people, roles, pending invites, and key verification status.
- **Insights**: activity by person and by tool, and knowledge-concentration warnings when only one person has touched a project.
- **Settings**: memory delivery (context block, recall on read, session summaries, MCP server), privacy (end-to-end sharing mode, verbatim-prompt sharing, redaction patterns, excluded folders), and the local daemon.

## Everything else it does

- **Cross-tool memory.** Claude Code and Codex share one store. Switching tools doesn't reset context.
- **Auto-registers over MCP.** Finds the agents you have installed and wires itself in.
- **Ask why about any file.** `membridge why file:line` shows which session touched a line, by whom, and the reasoning behind it: the question `git blame` cannot answer.
- **Per-project access control.** Pick exactly who sees which project, changed in one grid.
- **One-command onboarding.** A new teammate joins with a single invite link.
- **Roles and an audit trail.** Owner, admin, member. Every membership and sharing change recorded.
- **Health at a glance.** Who's syncing, whose keys are verified, and anything that quietly stopped reaching the team.
- **Runs local.** A daemon on each machine, bound to 127.0.0.1. No agent of ours in your CI, no repo upload.
- **It's just markdown.** Memory lands between `<!-- membridge -->` markers in `CLAUDE.md` and `AGENTS.md`; your own notes stay untouched, and `membridge remove` restores every file exactly.

## Privacy and what actually goes over the network

- Your sessions, summaries, and code stay on your machine unless you turn on team sync. There are no accounts and no API key to bring.
- Team sync is end-to-end encrypted, on by default. Keys are generated on each laptop and never leave it, so the backend stores ciphertext it cannot open. The content is what gets encrypted; routing details (author, project, timestamp, tool) stay readable so sync and access control can work.
- Verbatim prompts stay on your machine by default. Only summaries and file paths sync unless someone opts in, per session or per project.
- Secrets are stripped before anything is written to disk or synced: built-in patterns for AWS, GitHub, Google, Slack, OpenAI and Anthropic keys, JWTs, PEM blocks, connection strings with inline credentials, and bearer tokens, plus a high-entropy catch-all and your own patterns. Redaction runs at every boundary, including on data arriving back from teammates.
- Removing a teammate revokes access immediately and mints a new team key sealed only to the people who remain.
- Separate from your work content, MemBridge sends anonymous usage counters and diagnostics: a random install id, the version, and coarse feature-health signals, never code, file names, paths, or project names. Both turn off with the diagnostics setting (`diagnostics.enabled: false`) or `MEMBRIDGE_NO_DIAGNOSTICS=1`. It also asks GitHub's public releases API about once every six hours whether a newer release exists.
- The membridge.app site itself sets no cookies and runs no analytics scripts.

## Install

Two ways to run it:

**npm (macOS, Linux, Windows, Node 18+)**: one command, about two minutes, no account:

    npm install -g @membridgeai/membridge

**The app (macOS, Apple Silicon only)**: the desktop app bundles the daemon and CLI. There is no Windows or Intel Mac build of the app yet; on those machines the npm CLI works today. Download:

    https://github.com/MembridgeAi/membridge/releases/latest

Install on one repo and watch a session get distilled. Team sync is a separate, deliberate step. Teams can book a twenty-minute setup call on their own repository: hello@membridge.app.

## Frequently asked questions

### Does our code leave the machine?

No. MemBridge reads your agent sessions locally and writes memory to disk on the same machine. Your sessions, summaries and code go nowhere until you turn on team sync, and even then it is only what your sessions concluded: decisions, summaries, and file paths, never your source code. Team sync is end-to-end encrypted, so the backend stores ciphertext it has no key for. Separate from your work content, MemBridge sends anonymous usage counters and diagnostics tied to a random install id (turn them off with the diagnostics setting or MEMBRIDGE_NO_DIAGNOSTICS=1), and it asks GitHub about once every six hours whether a newer release exists.

### What happens to secrets that show up in a session?

They are stripped before anything is written to disk or sent to your team. MemBridge matches the shapes of AWS, GitHub, Google, Slack, OpenAI and Anthropic keys, JWTs, PEM blocks, connection strings with inline credentials, and bearer tokens, plus a high-entropy catch-all for the ones nobody has a pattern for. Redaction runs at every boundary, including on data arriving back from your teammates.

### How is this different from maintaining CLAUDE.md ourselves?

A hand-written context file is the startup half of this, and it only stays useful while somebody keeps editing it. MemBridge writes that file for you from what your sessions actually concluded. The two things it does that a file cannot: deliver a teammate's decision into a session that is already running, and answer a question against months of your team's history that no file would still contain.

### Which tools does it work with?

Claude Code and Codex are first class, and they share one memory, so switching tools mid-task doesn't reset anything. It registers itself over MCP with whichever agents it finds installed. Other agents that write session logs can be pointed at with a config entry.

### What happens when someone leaves the team?

Removing them revokes access to every shared project immediately and mints a new team encryption key sealed only to the people who remain, so their copy stops being able to read anything new. Membership and sharing changes are all recorded in an audit trail.

### Can people keep some work private?

Yes, at three levels. Verbatim prompts stay on your machine by default; only summaries and file paths sync unless someone opts in. Any project can be kept private, and shared projects have per-person access. A developer can pause capture entirely for a project without affecting anyone else.

### Do people have to change how they work?

No. It watches the sessions your team already runs and writes to the instruction files your agents already read. Nobody writes documentation for it, and nobody has to remember to record anything.

## The Context Ledger

MemBridge's 2026 baseline study of 6,104 real coding-agent sessions from 310 developers, using exact per-request API accounting: https://membridge.app/context-ledger/

- The median developer spends 31% of agent tokens on re-orientation: the agent re-reading, re-searching, and re-deriving context in a codebase it has already worked in. At the corpus level, re-orientation is $13,776 of the $56,666 measured, or 24.3% of everything spent.
- In repos with history, 53% of file reads repeat an earlier session's work.
- Orientation share stays stubbornly high with repo experience; agents do not learn their way around a codebase on their own.
- Shared memory recovers an estimated 6 to 8% of total agent spend, net of its own cost.
